questions.title: What is your general approach to designing enterprise architecture?
questions.quick: I start with outcomes and constraints, not technology: what the business must achieve, by when, with which budget, skills, compliance and existing systems. Then I turn quality needs into measurable non-functional requirements, list options, and record the choice in an ADR with its trade-offs. I prototype the riskiest assumption early, and finally test the design against failure, deployment and load scenarios before committing the team to it.
questions.revision: Outcomes and constraints first, measurable NFRs, options recorded in ADRs, prototype the riskiest assumption, then test against failure, deployment and load.
questions.detailed:
A good architecture approach is repeatable, so different teams get consistent answers and reviewers know what to expect.

## The sequence I follow

1. **Outcomes and constraints.** Which business result matters, what is fixed (budget, deadline, compliance, existing platforms, team skills) and what is negotiable.
2. **Non-functional requirements.** Convert vague wishes into numbers: availability, latency percentiles, recovery time, data residency, cost per transaction.
3. **Options and decisions.** Shortlist two or three realistic options, score them against the drivers, and write an **ADR** for each significant choice.
4. **Prototype the riskiest assumption.** A timeboxed spike on the integration, performance figure or unknown technology that could invalidate the design.
5. **Validate.** Walk the design through failure, deployment and load scenarios.
6. **Communicate and evolve.** Publish context, container and deployment views; revisit ADRs when assumptions change.

{{diagram:approach}}

## Validation scenarios

| Lens | Question asked |
|---|---|
| Failure | What happens when a dependency is slow, down or returns bad data? |
| Deployment | How is it released, rolled back and migrated without downtime? |
| Load | What breaks first at 10x traffic, and is that acceptable? |
| Security | Where are the trust boundaries and who can see which data? |
| Operability | Can the on-call engineer diagnose it at 3am? |

## Principles

- Choose the simplest design that meets the stated NFRs; add complexity only against a named driver.
- Make decisions reversible where cheap, and deliberate where not.
- Keep the design in a form the team can challenge, not a document that is approved once and forgotten.

## Common mistakes

- Picking technology before understanding constraints.
- NFRs such as "must be fast and scalable" with no number.
- Skipping prototypes for the one risky integration.
- Decisions held only in meetings, with no ADR, so they are relitigated.
followUps: How do you decide which assumption to prototype first?
What do you do when constraints conflict with each other?
How do you keep the architecture current after the first release?

diagrams.title: Architecture design approach
diagrams.alt: The approach starts with outcomes and constraints, moves to measurable non-functional requirements, then options and ADRs, a prototype of the riskiest assumption, validation against failure, deployment and load, and finally a feedback loop that revises decisions.

questions.title: How do you establish architecture standards across a global engineering team?
questions.quick: I separate a small set of mandatory guardrails, such as security, data handling and observability, from recommendations teams may adapt. I back them with reference architectures, templates and automated checks in the pipeline, so compliance is the easy path. Exceptions are allowed through a light process with an owner, rationale and review date. I measure impact with DORA-style delivery metrics and incident trends, and retire standards that do not help.
questions.revision: Few mandatory guardrails, many recommendations, reference templates, automated checks, time-boxed exceptions with owners, measured by DORA metrics and incidents.
questions.detailed:
Standards fail when they are documents nobody reads or gates nobody can pass. The aim is to make the right way the easiest way, without blocking teams.

## Two tiers

| Tier | Examples | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|
| **Mandatory guardrails** | Authentication, secrets handling, data classification, logging and tracing, dependency scanning | Automated checks, blocking |
| **Recommendations** | Framework choice, service layout, testing style | Reference material, advisory |

Keep the mandatory list short and justified by risk. Every rule should name the failure it prevents.

## Making compliance easy

- **Reference architectures** for common shapes (API service, event consumer, AI application).
- **Templates and starter repositories** with the guardrails already wired in.
- **Automated checks:** linting, policy-as-code, architecture fitness tests and pipeline gates.
- **Short ADRs** for decisions that depart from the reference.

## Exceptions

{{diagram:guardrails}}

An exception is recorded with an **owner**, the **rationale**, compensating controls and a **review date**. Expired exceptions are escalated, not silently renewed. Patterns of repeated exceptions are a signal the standard is wrong.

## Measuring

- **DORA-style metrics:** deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore.
- **Incident trends** attributable to standard areas, such as security findings or missing observability.
- **Adoption:** share of services on the templates, and exception count and age.

Review the standards quarterly with representatives from each region so they are co-owned, not imposed.

## Common mistakes

- Dozens of mandatory rules, so teams route around all of them.
- Standards without templates or tooling.
- Permanent exceptions with no owner.
- Central approval for everything, creating a bottleneck.
followUps: How do you get regional teams to co-own the standards?
What would you do if a standard slowed delivery measurably?
How do you decide whether a recommendation should become mandatory?

diagrams.title: Guardrails and exception flow
diagrams.alt: A team starts from a reference template and passes automated guardrail checks. If checks pass the change ships. If not, the team either fixes the issue or requests an exception with an owner, rationale and review date, which is reviewed, tracked and revisited on expiry.

questions.title: How would you design reusable platform components and accelerators for an AI Centre of Excellence?
questions.quick: I treat accelerators as products with users. I start from repeated needs seen across teams, such as retrieval, prompt evaluation, guardrails and model gateway access, and build them inner-source so teams can contribute. They are versioned with clear compatibility promises, offered as golden paths with templates and documentation, backed by a support model, and measured by adoption, time to first use and reuse rather than by how many components exist.
questions.revision: Build accelerators as products: demand-led, inner-source, semantically versioned, golden paths with docs, defined support, adoption metrics.
questions.detailed:
Reusable components only create value if other teams choose to use them. The design problem is as much about adoption as about code.

## Start from demand

Find what several teams are already rebuilding: model gateway, retrieval pipeline, evaluation harness, prompt and guardrail libraries, observability, cost tracking. Build the second use case before generalising; do not abstract from one example.

## Design principles

- **Golden paths:** an opinionated, supported route from idea to production, with escape hatches.
- **Inner-source:** the CoE owns the core, but teams contribute through pull requests, with clear contribution guidelines and review turnaround.
- **Versioning:** semantic versions, a deprecation policy, changelogs and compatibility tests so upgrades are predictable.
- **Composable and thin:** small libraries and templates, not a framework that forces everything.
- **Secure by default:** governance controls such as approved models, logging and data handling are built in.

{{diagram:platform}}

## Operating model

| Area | Practice |
|---|---|
| Documentation | Quickstart in under an hour, examples, decision guides |
| Support | Office hours, a channel with a response target, an issue tracker |
| Roadmap | Public backlog, prioritised by adoption demand |
| Quality | Tests, evaluation baselines, release notes |

## Adoption metrics

- Number of teams and services using each component.
- Time from first contact to first production use.
- Share of new AI projects starting on the golden path.
- Satisfaction feedback and support ticket volume.
- Components with no users are retired.

## Common mistakes

- Building a platform before any team has asked for it.
- Mandating use without making it better than the alternative.
- Breaking changes without notice or migration guides.
- No owner or support, so teams fork and diverge.
followUps: How do you decide when to retire a component?
What would you do if teams keep forking an accelerator?
How do you balance flexibility against a golden path?

diagrams.title: Accelerator lifecycle
diagrams.alt: Repeated team needs feed a CoE backlog. The CoE builds versioned components and golden-path templates in an inner-source repository. Product teams adopt them with documentation and support, contribute improvements back, and adoption metrics steer the roadmap.
